Dermatology · published research

Paronychia

In an eight-person randomized within-person study, red LED treatment reduced erythema, overall severity, and pain scores for EGFR-inhibitor-associated paronychia compared with the control side. Evidence for other causes of paronychia is absent.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In an eight-person randomized within-person study, red LED treatment reduced erythema, overall severity, and pain scores for EGFR-inhibitor-associated paronychia compared with the control side. Evidence for other causes of paronychia is absent.

Summary of the Evidence

One randomized, single-blind human study directly examined paronychia caused by epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor therapy. Eight participants were enrolled in a within-person comparison, with the red-light-treated side compared with a control side. No independent clinical cohort, review, animal study, or laboratory model is identified for this indication.

Human and clinical evidence

The study reported lower erythema, overall paronychia severity, and pain scores on the red-light-treated side at weeks 4, 6, and 8. The direction of change was therefore favorable across visible inflammation and discomfort, rather than limited to one measurement. Because participants served as their own comparison, differences between people are reduced, but the total sample remains eight and the study has not been independently replicated (Jornsamer et al. 2021).

The population had treatment-related nail-fold inflammation during EGFR-inhibitor therapy. The result does not directly address bacterial or fungal infection, trauma, chronic irritant exposure, or idiopathic paronychia. It also does not establish whether light treatment changes recurrence, antibiotic use, or decisions about cancer-drug dose modification.

Animal evidence

No animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No paronychia-specific cell or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The intervention was described as red LED treatment delivered two to three times weekly for six weeks. The accessible report and database record do not provide enough dosimetry to state the exact wavelength, irradiance, or energy per area with confidence. The evidence supports only this reported red-light protocol in EGFR-inhibitor-associated paronychia; it does not define a general dose for other nail-fold conditions.

Interpretation

The study found less redness, lower overall severity, and less pain on the treated side during follow-up. This is a favorable controlled observation in a specific medication-related condition. Its small size and lack of replication mean that the effect’s typical size and durability are not yet known.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term improvement in EGFR-inhibitor-associated paronychia
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A randomized within-person study found lower redness, severity, and pain on the red-light-treated side, giving a direct comparison in the target condition. It enrolled only eight people and has no independent replication, so the result is preliminary. A larger masked trial with clear dose reporting and follow-up after treatment would show whether the improvement is reproducible and lasting.
